national-airline-shutdown.headline: Another national airline shuts down and cancels all flights
national-airline-shutdown.body_md:
The seed headline for this piece names no carrier, and the one outlet it cites, TheStreet, runs a recurring "another national airline" series. TheStreet's pages could not be opened here, so the specific airline behind the headline could not be confirmed. What can be said is that several carriers have stopped flying within days of each other. The one with the clearest UK exposure is Norse Atlantic of Norway, which cancelled all flights on Wednesday. It is not a flag carrier, so the "national" label does not fit it.

## Norse Atlantic: the case with UK exposure

Norse Atlantic, a Norwegian low-cost long-haul operator, stopped flying on 25 November and halted bookings, according to One Mile at a Time and other travel outlets. Passengers were reportedly checking in when they learned the airline was grounded.

The company had warned of trouble in advance. It said: "The Company's financial situation is critical," and that it "is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs." It has said it is exploring strategic alternatives, including a possible takeover, ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance) contracts and short-term financing, and has given no assurance that any of these will work. It has not formally announced liquidation.

The fleet is 12 Boeing 787s, none of them owned. The aircraft would presumably go back to their lessors. Two of them flew for Pakistan International Airlines under a wet-lease arrangement, and PIA cancelled the London–Islamabad (PK786) and Manchester–Lahore (PK710) services, citing an "unexpected operational suspension" by its partner. These are the UK-facing casualties that have been confirmed so far. No passenger count has been published.

The business had been shrinking. The long-haul low-cost model it was built on had already failed, and it lost an IndiGo lease. One Mile at a Time links that loss to airspace closures and high fuel costs.

## The wider run of exits

Norse is one of several. Slovakia's AirExplore, a charter carrier, said it ceased operations on 10 November and applied to surrender its air operator's certificate. Armenian Airlines has told management it intends to surrender its certificate again, with high jet fuel prices given as the reason. TheStreet has also covered Congo Airways, whose future remains unclear after it stopped flying.

The common thread is cost. Jet fuel and airspace restrictions are squeezing carriers with thin balance sheets and leased fleets. These are mostly small or niche operators, and none is a large flag carrier. That keeps the failures in brief territory, but the pattern bears watching.

## What to watch

Three things will show how far this goes. The first is whether Norse finds financing or a buyer, or files for insolvency. The second is how PIA re-covers its UK routes. The third is whether Norse's lessors move to repossess the 787s. UK passengers with Norse-operated tickets should look to their booking channel. Package holidays carry ATOL cover, and card payments may offer Section 75 protection.
national-airline-shutdown.in_one_sentence: Several small carriers have stopped flying in recent days; Norse Atlantic is the one with UK exposure, after it grounded its 12-jet fleet and disrupted PIA's London and Manchester services.

eu-fees-reset-politics.headline: Burnham signals higher fees for EU students as Badenoch and Farage open fronts on the reset
eu-fees-reset-politics.body_md:
A headline in the Guardian says Andy Burnham has indicated that EU nationals would pay higher tuition fees at UK universities than UK students do. The day's other political coverage suggests his rivals have noticed. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, is reported to be challenging him over fees for EU students. Nigel Farage is reported to be helping launch a campaign against the UK rejoining the EU. None of the underlying articles could be read in full for this piece. What follows therefore sets out what is claimed, what the claim would mean if it holds, and what remains untested.

## The claim, and what is missing

The reported position is simple to state. EU students would be charged more than their UK counterparts. That is not in itself unusual. Since Brexit, EU nationals starting courses in England have generally been treated as international students, paying higher fees without access to the domestic loan system. On that footing, a pledge to charge EU students more would be a continuation of the status quo.

The framing in the source material suggests something different: that Burnham has *indicated* the policy as a deliberate stance, and that it would be read as a signal about how a Burnham-led government would approach the EU relationship. The distinction matters. If the reported position merely preserves current arrangements, it says little. If it rules out a reciprocal deal, such as the lower fees some in the sector have long argued for as part of a closer EU relationship, it says more.

The material supplied gives no date, quote or policy document. The sole source for the original claim is a single Guardian Politics headline. Until the wording of Burnham's remarks is on the record, the policy is a claim to be tested rather than a finding. It is unclear whether he was setting out a manifesto-style commitment, answering a question, or declining to rule something out.

## Badenoch's wedge

The second thread is political rather than administrative. Badenoch is reported, by BBC Politics and the Guardian, to be pressing Burnham on fees for EU students. The dispute is framed as connected both to the UK-EU reset and to Burnham's standing in the polls. No figures or specific charges have been supplied.

The logic of the attack is legible even without the detail. Fees are a concrete, household-level issue, and they let a Conservative leader test Labour-aligned figures on the reset in terms voters can picture. Whether Badenoch is attacking the policy as too harsh on Europeans, too soft on British taxpayers, or simply as evidence of inconsistency is not clear from what is available. The article texts were not checked, so that remains open.

## Farage reopens the argument

The third thread broadens the frame. Farage, who leads Reform UK, is reported by BBC Politics to be helping launch a campaign against the UK rejoining the EU. The campaign's name, funders and spokespeople are not in the material to hand. It is a single-source report.

The context is the reset itself. A separate item in this edition reports that the UK-EU treaties are expected to carry a 10-year break clause as Brussels tables its terms. A campaign against rejoining, launched while treaties are still being negotiated, suggests Farage wants Brexit to stay a live dividing line rather than a settled one. It also gives any Labour-leaning figure a reason to be careful about how a fee policy for Europeans sounds.

## What ties it together

Taken together, the threads show how a narrow policy point can carry a wider argument. Fees for EU students are a small line in the budget of most universities, but they stand in for a larger question: whether Britain treats European citizens as partners, as foreigners, or as something in between. Burnham's reported position, Badenoch's challenge and Farage's campaign each place that question in a different spot.

The next steps are practical. First, the exact words Burnham used need to be on the record, along with any accompanying policy paper. Second, any detail from universities or sector bodies on what higher EU fees would mean for recruitment would show whether this is a symbolic or a budgetary matter. Third, the terms of the UK-EU treaty negotiations will show whether student fees and mobility are on the table at all. If they are, the answer to how a Burnham-led government would treat the EU will come from the negotiating room rather than from a headline.
eu-fees-reset-politics.in_one_sentence: Burnham is reported to favour higher fees for EU students than UK ones, Badenoch and Farage are pressing the EU issue, but the claim rests on a single unverified headline.

eswatini-removal-death.headline: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after UK sent him to Eswatini
eswatini-removal-death.body_md:
A Sri Lankan man who was moved by the British government to Eswatini, a small landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, has died by suicide there. Kishanth Peramalya died on 13 September, according to reporting by the BBC and the Guardian that emerged this week. The case is not a conventional asylum removal. It is, however, a documented death after a UK-arranged transfer to a country with no connection to the person sent. That makes it a test of what the government owes people it relocates, and of how far third-country arrangements can be run without parliamentary scrutiny.

## From a stranded boat to Diego Garcia

Peramalya was among a group of Sri Lankans who left India by boat in 2021 hoping to reach Canada. The vessel got into difficulty in October 2021. The Royal Navy rescued those on board and took them to Diego Garcia, the British Indian Ocean Territory island that hosts a UK-US military base. The group stayed there for years in a camp that a critical UN report later described as unsuitable.

In November 2024 the UK allowed 61 of the migrants to travel to Britain. Peramalya was not among them. The then Home Secretary, Yvette Cooper, refused him entry on the basis of convictions recorded on the island: four counts of sexual assault, one of assault causing actual bodily harm, and one of arson. UK courts upheld that decision.

He could not simply be sent home. He had been protected from return to Sri Lanka because, as a teenager, he was tortured and sexually abused by members of the Sri Lankan military. A High Court judgment in February 2025 recorded that he had post-traumatic stress disorder and had made several suicide attempts on Diego Garcia. The government therefore faced a man it did not want to admit, could not return, and knew to be at serious risk of self-harm.

## The move to Eswatini

According to the BBC, the Maldives agreed in late March to host him for 30 days. He was then moved to Eswatini, which borders South Africa and Mozambique. The BBC reported a draft arrangement under which the UK would pay for his resettlement for three years, and that Britain was working on plans for him to stay permanently. The Guardian said it had not seen the draft.

Eswatini's government gives a different account. Its spokesperson, Thabile Mdluli, said the original arrangement was temporary, meant to protect him while the UK sought a lasting solution, and that the two governments never concluded a formal agreement on long-term residency. She declined to discuss his stay or death, and said Eswatini had received no other comparable request from the UK.

His family told the BBC that he was first housed alone in a secluded guesthouse and struggled with isolation, phoning his sister up to four times a day. His psychiatric appointments became daily as his condition worsened. His relatives said they had not known of his convictions, or that the move might become permanent.

A UK government spokesperson said public safety remained the government's foremost concern, including preventing people convicted of serious offences abroad from entering Britain, and that the UK continues to work with Eswatini on the case.

## Why it reaches beyond one case

Eswatini is not new to this kind of arrangement. Since July 2025 it has taken dozens of people deported from the United States who are not its nationals. In November 2025 its government confirmed it had received $5.1m to accept as many as 160 migrants from Washington. The pattern is one of small, dependent states paid to host people that larger ones will not.

Two caveats matter. Peramalya's case is unusual: his convictions, his protected status and his stay on a British overseas territory set it apart from ordinary asylum claims, and it does not by itself show how any wider UK removals scheme operates. And the reporting so far has not established what support was in place at the time of his death, or whether the draft terms were ever finalised.

What the case does raise is a duty-of-care question. The government's own courts had recorded his suicide risk. Whether a transfer to an isolated placement in an unfamiliar country, with a dispute between two governments over who was responsible for him, met that duty is likely to be tested.

## What to watch

Three things will decide how far this travels. Ministers may face questions in Parliament about the unpublished arrangements, which the BBC described as never having been disclosed to MPs. An inquest or investigation in Eswatini or the UK, if opened, would set out what monitoring and psychiatric care existed. And lawyers acting for the family could use the case to challenge future transfers on grounds of known risk to health. The government has so far said only that it is working with Eswatini.
eswatini-removal-death.in_one_sentence: Kishanth Peramalya, a Sri Lankan man with documented suicide risk, died in Eswatini on 13 September after a UK-arranged transfer, raising duty-of-care and transparency questions.

netanyahu-charges-recommendation.headline: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
netanyahu-charges-recommendation.body_md:
The judges hearing Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial said on Wednesday that prosecutors should consider dropping the most serious of the three cases against him. They also said another case may not describe a crime at all. The remarks were not a ruling. They went to the attorney general, who alone decides whether the prosecution goes ahead, and they did not go to the president's office. That differs from the framing in the triage notes for this piece, which suggested the matter would be routed to a political pardon process. The reporting reviewed here does not support that, and the pardon track is a separate matter that has been running for a year.

## What the judges said

Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three linked cases. The trial began in 2020 and has been repeatedly delayed. He has denied all the charges and calls the prosecution a political witch hunt.

According to accounts of Wednesday's hearing, the panel's remarks fell into three parts:

- **Case 4000, the bribery case.** Prosecutors allege Netanyahu gave regulatory favours to the telecoms group Bezeq, reportedly worth about 1.8bn shekels (about $500m). In return, they say, he received favourable coverage on a news site owned by the group's controlling shareholder. The judges said bribery and conflict of interest would be hard to prove and that the chances of conviction were low. They asked the attorney general to consider dropping the bribery charge.
- **Case 2000.** This concerns an alleged deal with a newspaper owner that never materialised. The judges expressed serious doubt that any offence was committed.
- **Case 1000.** Prosecutors allege Netanyahu accepted nearly $300,000 in gifts, including cigars and champagne, from the film producer Arnon Milchan and the billionaire James Packer between 2007 and 2016. In return, they say, he tried to extend a tax exemption for Milchan and help him renew a US visa. The judges said this case could be brought to a conclusion, which was read as pointing towards a plea agreement.

The suggestion is not new in kind. In 2023 the same bench proposed that prosecutors consider dropping the bribery charge, and prosecutors declined. In June, after Netanyahu finished testifying, the judges again indicated that bribery would be hard to establish. Wednesday's remarks go further because they cover all three cases and come at the end of the evidence.

## Who decides

Israeli courts do not drop charges. Only the prosecution can withdraw them, and the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, sits at the top of that chain. She told the court that she and her team would consider the judges' comments and remained open to all options. For Case 1000 she described the options as a verdict or a plea deal. If the cases continue, the same judges would issue the verdict unless a plea agreement is reached.

Netanyahu's response was immediate. In a televised statement he said "today, the trial has fallen" and that it "must end immediately." He called the judges' remarks a "ray of truth and justice." That reading goes beyond what the bench said. The panel questioned two cases, and it pointed the third towards a possible settlement, which usually involves some admission of wrongdoing. It did not suggest that the whole prosecution should end.

## The pardon track

The president's office is still involved, though through a different route. A year ago Netanyahu formally asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon, with public backing from Donald Trump. Herzog did not grant it. He offered to start a mediation process towards a plea deal instead. Herzog has said the attorney general was ready for talks and that Netanyahu's representatives had not responded.

A Justice Ministry pardons unit reportedly found the request did not meet the necessary conditions. It reportedly said a pardon would be appropriate only if he resigned, confessed or was convicted. Bloomberg reported in April that Herzog had put the request aside for now.

The judges' remarks could change that. If the attorney general drops Case 4000 and narrows the rest, the argument for a pardon weakens, because the pressure that prompted the request eases. If she does not, the judges' comments give Netanyahu's camp a public statement from the bench that it can use to press for a deal on better terms.

## Political stakes

The timing matters. Netanyahu and his allies failed to win a parliamentary majority in last month's election. The centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has been given the first chance to form a government. Most mainstream parties have refused to sit with a prime minister who is on trial. A material narrowing of the charges would weaken that objection, though it would not remove it. Case 1000 could still end in a conviction or a plea deal.

The longer-running conflict between the government and the judiciary is also in play. Netanyahu's allies have attacked the attorney general and the courts for years. A decision by Baharav-Miara to keep the bribery charge against the bench's advice would draw sharp criticism from them. A decision to drop it would draw criticism from opponents who say the prosecution was sound.

## What to watch

The first marker is the attorney general's formal response to the court, which will show whether she drops Case 4000, narrows Case 2000 or keeps both. The second is whether Netanyahu's lawyers answer Herzog's mediation offer. The third is the coalition talks under Eisenkot, where the status of the trial will bear on who can sit in government.

A caveat on sourcing: the account here draws on reports of the hearing, including wire-agency copy carried by regional outlets, and the BBC original was not available for direct comparison. The judges' exact wording on each case should be checked against the court record.
netanyahu-charges-recommendation.in_one_sentence: Judges in Netanyahu's trial urged prosecutors to consider dropping the bribery case and questioned another, but the attorney general decides, and the president's pardon track is separate.

us-new-tariffs-china.headline: US announces new tariffs on a host of countries, including China
us-new-tariffs-china.body_md:
The United States has proposed a fresh round of tariffs on China and 13 other trading partners, a measure that would reach well beyond Beijing. Announced on 25 November, the plan is a proposal rather than a law. Duties are unlikely to bite for some months. Even so, it is the clearest sign yet of how Washington intends to rebuild its tariff wall after the courts took apart the old one.

## What has been proposed

The proposals rest on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The United States Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, says an investigation opened in March 2026 found that the targeted economies sustain manufacturing capacity beyond what their own markets need. Of the 14 economies, [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/25/us-tariffs-trump-section-301.html) names four: China, the European Union, Japan and India. Other coverage points to Brazil, Taiwan and Vietnam among the rest. The full list should be checked against the USTR's own notice.

Most proposed rates fall between 15% and 20%. China would face 20%, on top of existing Section 301 duties of roughly 25% imposed over forced technology transfer. That would take tariffs on many Chinese goods to about 45%. Some reports suggest a higher ceiling, up to 40% on the new tranche, if talks with Beijing fail. That figure is not consistently reported and should be treated cautiously.

Greer sought to soften the arithmetic. The rates, he said, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on existing duties. "In effect, it'll look more like a top up," he said. China's foreign ministry rejected the premise: "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," it said.

## Why Section 301, and why now

The choice of statute is the story's backbone. The Supreme Court struck down the earlier sweeping tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. A stopgap 10% duty under Section 122 then lapsed after its 150-day limit. Section 301 is slower and more procedural. It requires an investigation, findings, public comment and hearings. It is also sturdier in court, which is presumably the point. The administration has also used the same statute in separate forced-labour investigations covering 60 economies, which produced tariffs of 10% to 12.5%.

The timing is awkward for Beijing. The proposal arrives about a week after a Trump-Xi summit, and the [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3375801/us-proposes-new-20-tariffs-china-week-after-trump-xi-summit) reports that it is unlikely on its own to upend the truce struck at Busan last year. A proposed tariff with months of process ahead is also a bargaining chip, and the summit's afterglow may be part of what is being tested.

## The timetable

No effective date has been set. Greer said he did not think any of the duties would take effect "earlier than a couple months from now". Hearings and a comment period come first, and some outlets report January as the earliest realistic start. The precise dates for those hearings were not stated in the reporting reviewed, and reports differ on when the current China truce expires. Final rates may differ from those proposed.

## What it means for UK exporters

The UK is not among the economies named in the coverage reviewed, and CNBC's report does not mention it. The exposure for FTSE-listed exporters is therefore indirect, and it runs through three channels.

The first is supply chains. UK-listed manufacturers that source components from China, Vietnam, India or the EU and sell finished goods into the American market could face higher costs if their inputs or their European plants fall within scope. The second is diversion. Chinese and other exporters hit by 20% duties may redirect goods to Europe and other markets, adding pricing pressure for British producers at home and abroad. The third is demand. A wider tariff list adds to uncertainty for American importers and could dampen orders.

Those effects cannot be sized until the product lists are published. The proposed rates are headline figures, and the damage depends on which tariff lines are covered. Whether any FTSE company is materially exposed will turn on that detail.

## What to watch

The next markers are the USTR's formal notice and product lists, the dates of the public hearings and comment deadline, and any Chinese response before the truce deadline. A legal challenge is likely, given the way the previous tariffs ended. Until the lists appear, the plan is best read as an opening position, not a settled policy.

conversion-practices-ban.headline: Labour 'committed' to conversion practices ban despite calls to scrap it
conversion-practices-ban.body_md:
Labour is standing by its pledge to outlaw conversion practices in England and Wales, even as critics press ministers to abandon the proposed law. The government has described itself as "committed" to a ban, according to reporting by the Guardian. The argument is now less about whether the measure is wanted than about whether a government with a large majority and a crowded legislative timetable will keep a promise that has already outlasted several prime ministers.

## A promise with a long history

Conversion practices are attempts to change or suppress a person's sexual orientation or gender identity. They range from organised "therapy" to pressure exerted within religious or family settings. Banning them was first promised by Theresa May's government in 2018, after a national LGBT survey found that a notable minority of respondents had been offered or had undergone such treatment.

The pledge then stalled. Boris Johnson's government confirmed a ban in 2021, retreated in 2022 to a version covering sexual orientation only, and never put a bill before Parliament. The reversals left the subject politically charged. For campaigners, the delay was evidence of reluctance. For opponents, the shifting scope showed how hard the underlying questions are.

Labour's 2024 manifesto promised to deliver a ban that was inclusive of trans people. That wording matters, because the inclusion of gender identity is where most of the dispute lies.

## Where the objections come from

Critics of the proposed law tend to raise three kinds of concern. The first is definitional: that a statute broad enough to catch coercive practices could also reach ordinary conversations between clergy, counsellors, parents and young people. The second is clinical: that clinicians treating children and teenagers who are questioning their gender could fear prosecution for cautious, exploratory approaches. The third is that existing criminal law on assault, coercion and harassment already covers the worst abuses.

Supporters answer that the worst practices are well documented, that existing offences are hard to apply when the harm is psychological and the setting is religious or domestic, and that carve-outs for consensual, non-coercive support can be written into the bill. Drafting is therefore the real battleground. The detail of how a ban defines "practice", how it treats consent and what protections it gives to counselling and pastoral care will decide whether the legislation is workable.

## What the government is signalling

Holding the line is a choice with a price. A contested bill takes up parliamentary time, and ministers have other business to protect. Dropping it would break a manifesto commitment and would be read as a concession on the question of trans inclusion. The decision to restate the pledge publicly suggests ministers have judged that backing away would cost more than pressing on.

The pledge says nothing about timing, however. A commitment to a ban is different from a date for a bill, and this one has so far been expressed as the former. Devolved administrations are also moving at different speeds on their own approaches, which adds pressure for a consistent position across the UK.

## What to watch

The test will be whether a draft bill is published, and what it says about scope. Publication of draft text would allow scrutiny by a parliamentary committee, which is where the definitional arguments would be fought out in detail. Until then, "committed" remains a statement of intent that campaigners will measure against the legislative calendar.
conversion-practices-ban.in_one_sentence: Labour says it remains committed to banning conversion practices despite calls to scrap the proposed law, leaving scope and timing as the real fault lines.

no10-influencer-row-social-spend.headline: No 10 won't rule out re-inviting influencer at centre of 'vile video' row as social media unit spend set to double
no10-influencer-row-social-spend.body_md:
Downing Street has declined to rule out inviting back the online influencer at the centre of a row over a video that has been described as 'vile'. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to apologise for the video. That has turned a short-lived controversy into a question about how far No 10 is prepared to court the creators it has cultivated, and whether it will keep doing so.

The detail available so far is thin. The Guardian and BBC political desks report that Burnham will not apologise and that No 10 has not closed the door on a return invitation. Neither the triage notes nor the searches run for this piece turned up a verbatim Downing Street line or a full account of the video's contents. This article therefore sticks to what is reported and does not characterise the video itself.

## A government that courts creators

The row sits within a wider strategy. Burnham's team has leaned heavily on TikTok, podcasts and informal formats. Commentators have called him Britain's first 'TikTok prime minister', and one report says No 10 has told him to tone down his 'blokey' pub antics. Inviting influencers into Downing Street is part of the same approach: it reaches audiences that conventional briefings do not.

The cost of that approach is that the government shares a platform with people over whom it has little control. Refusing to rule out a repeat invitation keeps the channel open. It also means the government is not distancing itself from someone it has already hosted. Burnham's refusal to apologise points the same way, though a spokesperson's non-answer is not the same as a decision to invite the person again.

## The money behind the megaphone

Separately, the BBC reports that spending on the government's social media operation is set to double to £25m, at a time when ministers' communications are under scrutiny. The report does not give the baseline or the period covered. Doubling to £25m implies a current budget of about £12.5m. That is close to the £13.2m annual messaging budget that Civil Service World reported for the New Media Unit, which has about 20 staff. A parliamentary answer gave a lower planned spend of £10.9m. The figures may not be like for like, and the unit named in the BBC report has not been confirmed as the same one.

Government departments that disclosed their figures have also reported spending about £2.1m on influencers since the 2024-25 financial year began, according to LBC. The true total is probably higher, because some departments declined to disclose.

## Informing or promoting

The two threads meet on one question. Public money spent on the government's own channels can be justified as public information: campaigns on health, benefits or safety delivered where people actually spend their time. Critics will say the larger the budget, the more it looks like promotion of ministers. Paid or favoured relationships with influencers sharpen that concern, because audiences may not distinguish a public-information message from a political one.

The row has limited reach beyond Westminster, and it is not a market story. Its significance is as a test of how a government that has built its presentation around online personalities handles one of them when the association becomes awkward.

What to watch: whether No 10 gives a clearer answer on future invitations, and whether the £25m figure is confirmed with a baseline and a time period. A published breakdown of how much of it goes to influencers would show whether the spending is mostly information or mostly promotion.

russia-high-speed-rail.headline: Russia presses on with Moscow-St Petersburg high-speed line despite railway debt crisis
russia-high-speed-rail.body_md:
Russia is pressing ahead with a high-speed railway between Moscow and St Petersburg even as the state-owned railway operator carries heavy debt. The report, from the business outlet IntelliNews, offers a picture of priorities more than of finances. The line is a flagship of the state, and the balance sheet of the company that must help pay for it has not stopped it.

The report is thin on detail. It gives no total for the operator's borrowings, no cost for the project and no statement from the government or Russian Railways. Those gaps matter, and the account below is limited to what can be said with confidence.

## A project with a long history

A fast link between Russia's two largest cities has been discussed, in one form or another, for well over a decade. The two cities lie roughly 650 kilometres apart, and the existing corridor already carries some of the busiest passenger services in the country. A purpose-built line would cut journey times sharply, and officials have long presented it as the centrepiece of a wider high-speed network.

The idea has also repeatedly run into the question of who pays. Projects of this kind are expensive almost everywhere. They depend on a mix of state budget money, borrowing by the operator and, in some models, private or sovereign-fund capital. How Russia intends to combine these is exactly what the IntelliNews report does not set out.

## Decision or drift?

The report supports two readings, and the evidence does not separate them.

The first is that this is a deliberate choice. A state that regards a project as strategic will fund it regardless of the operator's leverage, using the budget or the National Wealth Fund to cover what the railway cannot borrow. Debt at a state company is, on this view, a secondary concern.

The second is drift. Large projects acquire momentum: contracts are signed, land is cleared, and stopping becomes politically and administratively harder than continuing. A railway with heavy debt can find itself committed to spending without a settled funding plan.

Telling them apart would require the numbers: the size of the debt, its maturity and cost, the project's budget and the share that the state has committed. Without them, the report shows only that work continues.

## The wider squeeze

The backdrop is a Russian budget under strain. Defence spending is high, and borrowing costs have been elevated. In that setting, any flagship civil project becomes a test of whether the state will protect long-term infrastructure while it is short of money elsewhere. A line that proceeds despite its sponsor's debt would suggest that it will, at least for projects with symbolic weight. It would also suggest that the cost is being pushed onto the state's balance sheet, where it is harder to see.

That inference is a hypothesis, not a finding. The claims rest on a single outlet, and the figures that would confirm them have not been published.

## What to watch

The useful evidence will come from Russian Railways' next financial disclosures, which should show debt and investment spending, and from the federal budget documents, which would reveal any state funding committed to the line. A published cost estimate and financing plan would settle whether this is a decision or drift. Until those appear, the story remains unverified.
russia-high-speed-rail.in_one_sentence: Russia reportedly keeps building its Moscow–St Petersburg high-speed line while the state railway carries heavy debt, though the single-source report gives no figures.

single-stalking-offence.headline: Ministers to create single stalking offence, scrapping need to prove fear or distress
single-stalking-offence.body_md:
The UK government intends to fold its separate stalking offences into one, and to drop the requirement that prosecutors prove the victim felt fear or distress. That is the substance of reports from BBC UK and the Guardian UK. The detail below comes largely from secondary summaries, because the primary announcement text was not available to this writer. Specifics beyond the headline should be read with that in mind.

## The law as it stands

Stalking was made a specific crime in England and Wales in 2012, when the Protection of Freedoms Act added offences to the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. The structure has two tiers. A basic offence covers a course of conduct that amounts to stalking. A more serious offence covers stalking that causes the victim to fear violence, or that causes serious alarm or distress with a substantial effect on their day-to-day life.

The serious tier carries the heavier penalty, and it is also the one where the victim's reaction becomes part of what must be proved. Campaigners have long argued that this puts the wrong person under examination. A determined stalker who leaves a victim frightened may be easier to convict than one whose target has learnt to hide the effect, or whose conduct is controlling rather than overtly menacing.

## What is reported

The reports describe a single standalone offence in place of the current split, with the fear-or-distress test removed. Aggregated coverage links the plan to a review led by the barrister Richard Wright, and to the case of Alice Ruggles, the young woman killed by a former partner in 2016 after he had stalked her. Her family is reported to have welcomed the change.

Some points remain unsettled. Accounts conflict on the maximum sentence: one says up to 10 years, another says the government has decided not to raise the existing maximum. This article does not state a figure. No legislative timetable has been given; the Home Office is reported to have said a bill will follow when parliamentary time allows. The Victims' Commissioner is reported to have welcomed the single offence while arguing that the government had missed a chance to deal with stalking that continues after a conviction.

## What to watch

The test will be the drafting. Removing a fear-or-distress requirement shifts the weight onto what the defendant did and what they knew or ought to have known. Other jurisdictions have wrestled with the same question: New Zealand's reform debate has turned on whether prosecutors should have to prove what a stalker knew, and Ireland has kept a fear-based test in its own standalone offence. How narrowly or broadly Westminster defines the conduct, and what defences it allows for lawful or reasonable behaviour, will decide whether the change helps victims in practice or invites challenge. The first marker is the publication of a bill, or of the Home Office's own statement, which should settle the sentencing question.
single-stalking-offence.in_one_sentence: UK ministers plan to merge stalking offences into one and drop the need to prove victim fear or distress, though details such as sentencing and timetable remain unconfirmed.

tube-strike-begins.headline: London commuters face disruption as tube strike begins
tube-strike-begins.body_md:
A strike by London Underground drivers began on Thursday, closing or cutting back service across the Tube network and pushing commuters onto buses, the Elizabeth line and the Overground. It is the first of eight 24-hour walkouts that the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) has called between now and February 2027.

## What is closed

National Rail's disruption notice says the Circle and Piccadilly lines have no service all day. Other lines run normally until about 10:00 and are then reduced. From noon every line is disrupted, and the Waterloo & City line stops altogether. After 21:00 no Underground line runs. Recovery will be slow. The Circle, Piccadilly and Waterloo & City lines stay shut until noon on Friday, and normal service is not expected on all lines until about 18:00.

The Elizabeth line, DLR, Overground, buses and trams are running as normal, but are expected to be much busier than usual.

## The dispute

The row is over a proposal from Transport for London to let drivers compress their hours into a four-day week. The RMT calls the plan damaging. In a statement it said: "London Underground must withdraw these damaging proposals and engage seriously with the union." London Underground's Nick Dent says drivers "can now choose to remain on a five-day week with a guarantee of remaining at the same depot". The rival drivers' union Aslef is reported to have accepted the roster changes. That leaves the RMT the only union opposing them.

The drivers' action is separate from a Piccadilly line dispute involving the TSSA union. That one concerns the dismissal of an employee for gross misconduct, which the union says was unfair.

## The cost to the city

No one has yet published a figure for what this strike will cost London's economy. The most concrete evidence comes from last year. Dee Corsi of the New West End Company said West End sales fell by as much as 20% year on year on certain days during the 2025 strikes. She added that about half of West End visitors arrive by Underground, and that "any disruption to the network has an immediate and significant impact on local businesses."

The calendar is what worries hospitality. Allen Simpson of UKHospitality said the timing "will be particularly damaging, with two falling in the crucial trading period just before Christmas." The two dates are 17 and 19 December.

## What follows

The RMT has announced further 24-hour stoppages, each starting at noon, on 17 and 19 December, 4 and 6 January, and 17 and 23 February. National Rail's notice lists these six; a reported eighth date in late February is not on that list. The next checkpoint is whether talks produce a withdrawal or a change to the four-day proposal before the pre-Christmas dates. If they do not, the December strikes will show whether this dispute amounts to more than a local nuisance for London's retailers and restaurants.
tube-strike-begins.in_one_sentence: RMT drivers began the first of eight 24-hour Tube strikes over a four-day-week plan, with two more walkouts due in the run-up to Christmas.

nvidia-huang-probe.headline: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang faces reported attorney-general probe
nvidia-huang-probe.body_md:
A report that a US state attorney general is looking into Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has drawn more commentary than confirmed detail. Nobody has publicly said what the inquiry concerns, which office is running it, or on whose authority it was reported. The attorney general has declined to answer questions about it.

That gap defines the story. A declined question is not a denial, and it is not a confirmation either. Prosecutors' offices routinely refuse to say whether an investigation exists, and a refusal on its own carries no information about whether there is anything to find.

## What is reported, and what is not

The reporting, as it has reached this desk, says an attorney general is examining Huang or Nvidia. It does not establish:

- which state, or whether the office is state or federal;
- the conduct under examination, whether commercial, regulatory or personal;
- whether the inquiry targets Huang individually or the company;
- the on-record source for any of it.

The Bot Tribune has not been able to verify any of these points independently. Until one of them is pinned down, the probe is best read as a report rather than an established fact. Nvidia has not, in the material reviewed, been quoted either confirming or rejecting it.

## Why a probe would matter

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has been its chief executive ever since, which is more than three decades in one seat. Few leaders of companies this large are so closely identified with their firm's strategy and public image. Nvidia's chips sit at the centre of the AI build-out, and the stock carries heavy weight in major equity indices.

That is the basis for the commentary asking whether Huang is irreplaceable. The argument runs that a company so tied to one executive has a key-person risk, and that any legal cloud over him becomes a governance question for shareholders and index holders alike. It is a fair question in the abstract. It is a speculative one at present, because the commentary rests on an inquiry whose nature is unknown. A routine information request and a serious criminal matter would carry very different consequences, and the reports do not say which this is.

The timing also matters for markets. US stocks have been under pressure on worries about the AI boom, and the biggest AI names have been the focus of those worries. A story about the leader of the sector's bellwether lands in a nervous tape, which may amplify attention beyond what the known facts justify.

## What to watch

Three things would turn this from a report into a story. The first is a named, on-record confirmation from the attorney general's office of the existence and scope of an inquiry. The second is a statement from Nvidia, which would be expected if the matter were material enough to require disclosure. The third is any filing: Nvidia's next quarterly report, or an 8-K, would be the place a material legal proceeding involving the company would have to appear.

Until one of those arrives, the sound position is the narrow one: something has been reported, an official has not answered, and the question of Huang's indispensability is being asked ahead of the facts that would make it pressing.
nvidia-huang-probe.in_one_sentence: An attorney general reportedly probing Nvidia's Jensen Huang has declined to answer questions, and the allegation, office and source remain unverified.

huawei-trade-secrets-verdict.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
huawei-trade-secrets-verdict.body_md:
A federal jury in Brooklyn has split its verdict on Huawei. It found the Chinese telecoms group guilty of conspiring to steal American trade secrets. It cleared the company of racketeering, the sweeping charge that framed the whole prosecution as a two-decade criminal enterprise.

The outcome is a partial win for the US Justice Department. The case was built to show that Huawei's rise rested on a pattern of crime. The jury accepted that specific crimes happened. It did not accept that they added up to a racketeering enterprise.

## What the jury was asked to decide

The case was heard before US District Judge Ann Donnelly. Huawei Technologies and three affiliated companies faced 12 counts: racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and obstruction of justice. The racketeering count alleged a conspiracy running for about two decades.

Prosecutors, led in court by Assistant US Attorney Meredith Arfa, argued that Huawei built its international business through crimes against American companies, banks and the government. They said the company encouraged staff to obtain competitors' confidential technology, including from Cisco and T-Mobile. One example was information about Tappy, T-Mobile's smartphone-testing robot. They also alleged that Huawei hid its control of Skycom, a company operating in Iran, and misled HSBC and other banks about it.

The defence, led by Brian Heberlig, said the government had distorted ordinary business practice. It credited Huawei's success to engineering and investment. It said any misconduct was the work of individual employees who were later disciplined or fired. It also argued that some of the allegedly stolen material was publicly available, and that the banks knew about Huawei's Iran activity.

The jury heard about two months of testimony, from more than 60 prosecution witnesses and about 15 for the defence. It began deliberating on 18 November.

## Why the racketeering acquittal matters

Racketeering is the charge that turns a set of separate offences into one organised enterprise. To convict, a jury must find a pattern of criminal acts carried out through the company as a whole. That is a heavier claim than showing that employees took confidential material, and it is a harder one to prove.

The acquittal suggests the jury was willing to hold Huawei responsible for particular acts but not to accept the company-as-criminal-enterprise story. That fits the defence's central argument, that wrongdoing sat with individuals and not with the corporate structure. The jury's reasoning has not been published. This reading is an inference from the split, not a finding.

For prosecutors elsewhere, the practical lesson is about charging. Racketeering statutes give broad reach, including a long time horizon and a single narrative. A jury can reject that narrative and still convict on narrower counts. Cases against other China-linked technology firms may lean more on the specific counts.

## What is not yet confirmed

The headline outcome, a conviction on trade-secret theft and an acquittal on racketeering, matches the BBC's technology coverage. A legal-commentary report on the trial goes further. It says the jury convicted Huawei on 10 of the 12 counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud and sanctions violations, and also acquitted it of conspiracy to obstruct justice. That report is only partly visible and has not been checked against court records. Treat the full count-by-count breakdown as provisional.

Sentencing dates, any fine and Huawei's response were not available at the time of writing. A corporation cannot be jailed, so penalties would come as fines, probation terms and possible compliance conditions. Huawei has long denied wrongdoing, and an appeal is the usual next step after a conviction.

## What to watch

The next markers are the sentencing schedule set by Judge Donnelly, any post-trial motions from the defence seeking to overturn the convictions, and whether prosecutors say anything about the racketeering acquittal. Together they will show how much of the Justice Department's original case survives.

met-office-fewer-frosts.headline: Met Office: expect fewer frosts and more hot days as UK seasons shift
met-office-fewer-frosts.body_md:
The Met Office expects the UK to see fewer frosts and more hot days as its seasons shift, according to a climate-trend analysis reported by the BBC. The direction is clear. The size of the change, which decides how much it matters, was not given in the summary this article draws on.

The Met Office's own record already points the same way. Its published climate statistics show a warming UK over recent decades, and frost is one of the first things to thin out as winters warm. Hot days are the mirror image: as average summer temperatures rise, the upper tail of the distribution moves with them.

## What is claimed, and what is not

Two claims are reported. The first is that frost days are declining while hot days are increasing. The second is that this trend carries consequences for energy demand, agriculture and infrastructure.

No baseline or projected figures accompany either claim in the material available here. Those figures include the number of frost days per year, the threshold used to define a "hot day", the reference period, and the emissions scenario behind any projection. Without them the headline is a direction of travel, not a measurement. This article therefore quotes no numbers it could not check.

## Why the sectors named matter

**Energy.** A warmer winter would lower peak heating demand. Britain's gas-heated housing stock makes that a large lever. Hotter summers push the other way, because air conditioning remains uncommon in UK homes and offices. Any rise in summer cooling load would arrive on a grid built around winter peaks, so the net effect on demand and on capacity planning depends on how fast cooling is adopted.

**Agriculture.** Fewer frosts can lengthen growing seasons and reduce late-frost damage to blossom. The same shift can also bring heat stress, drier soils and new pest pressure, and some crops need winter chill to set fruit. The gains and the losses would not be evenly spread across crops or regions. Food prices are already a live concern, as the Bank of England's latest Financial Stability Report makes plain.

**Infrastructure.** Rail, roads and buildings in the UK were largely designed to older climate norms. Rails buckle and tarmac softens in extreme heat, and overheating in schools and hospitals is a recurring problem. Fewer freeze-thaw cycles would ease some winter maintenance, but that is unlikely to offset heat-related costs.

## What to watch

The useful test of this analysis is the detail behind it: the frost and hot-day counts, the baseline period and the scenarios used. The Met Office's annual State of the UK Climate report, normally published in summer, is the next scheduled point at which those trends are updated against observed data. Until the underlying figures are published and checked, the claim stands as a credible direction, not a quantified forecast.
met-office-fewer-frosts.in_one_sentence: A Met Office trend analysis reportedly points to fewer UK frosts and more hot days, with implications for energy, farming and infrastructure, though no figures were available to verify.

spacex-million-satellites.headline: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites into orbit
spacex-million-satellites.body_md:
The US Federal Communications Commission has cleared SpaceX to launch up to one million satellites, each a small orbital computer, in what would be the first data-centre constellation in space. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr announced the approval on Wednesday 25 November. Elon Musk replied on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The system, called Starmind, is a licence to try rather than a working network. No Starmind satellite has flown, and SpaceX has not said how much of the plan it expects to build.

## What the FCC actually approved

SpaceX filed its application on 30 January, soon after it acquired the AI company xAI. The Space Bureau accepted it for comment in early February. The authorisation covers up to one million satellites at altitudes of 500 km to 1,002 km. Each satellite would carry a computing payload averaging 175 kW, peaking at 250 kW, powered by solar arrays based on Starlink's design and cooled by deployable liquid radiators, according to trade outlet Via Satellite. Data would move mainly over optical links between satellites. Ka-band radio, under Starlink's existing authorisation, is limited to backup and emergency use. Some bands carry waivers and must run on an "unprotected" and non-interference basis.

The licence runs for 15 years from the first Starmind launch and sets milestones, per Via Satellite:

- one satellite by 25 November 2033
- 10% of the fleet by 25 November 2035
- 50% by 25 November 2038
- the full million by 25 November 2040

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell has said launches should begin in 2027.

The approval itself says little about the number of satellites SpaceX must actually build. Milestones of this kind are common in satellite licences, and operators have missed them before. Amazon is already behind on its own deployment targets, a point Carr made when answering its objections.

## The objections that were overruled

Amazon's Kuiper unit (now Amazon Leo), Viasat and the American Astronomical Society all petitioned to deny the application. Amazon called Starmind a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan" and said SpaceX would need "centuries" to build it. The FCC replied that questions of feasibility and business viability fall outside its mandate and declined to substitute its judgment for the applicant's.

The agency also dismissed concerns about atmospheric effects from satellites burning up on re-entry as "speculative and not supported in the record". It required no further National Environmental Policy Act review and brushed aside worries about optical astronomy. It said it does not cap the number of stations it can authorise in similar orbits, so congestion did not block the approval. Earthjustice's Jan Hasselman criticised both the skipped environmental review and the timing, in a holiday week. Astrophysicist Adam Becker warned of "a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions". The Secure World Foundation had urged a phased, demonstration-based approach, calling constellations of this size a "qualitative shift".

For scale, roughly 15,000 satellites currently operate in orbit, according to figures cited around the filing. One million is about 65 times that.

## Why compute people are watching

The pitch is that space offers near-constant sunlight and no land or grid constraints. SpaceX argued in its filing that orbital data centres are "the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power". Analysts quoted by Via Satellite say the concept remains technically and economically unproven. Heat rejection, radiation damage to chips and the cost of getting hardware up and replacing it are the open questions. Nothing in the approval tests those.

The approval does matter for competitors. Google's Project Suncatcher put its first AI chips into orbit in October, on a SpaceX rocket and a Planet Labs satellite. Blue Origin has asked the FCC for up to 51,600 satellites under Project Sunrise, and Starcloud has applied for 88,000. The FCC says it will decide those "expeditiously". If the agency treats Starmind as precedent, the first such approval was also the largest.

The spectrum side is narrower than the headline suggests. Because the links are mostly optical, Starmind leans less on scarce radio bands than a conventional broadband constellation does. That may help explain why the radio-spectrum objections did not carry the day.

## What to watch

The first test is the 2027 launch schedule, which will show whether a 175 kW satellite exists as hardware. The second is whether the FCC's pending decisions on Blue Origin and Starcloud adopt the same light-touch approach to debris and environmental review. The third is whether Amazon, Viasat or the astronomers seek reconsideration or take the matter to court. None has said so.

dart-asteroid-crater.headline: Images of asteroid hit in planetary-defence test reveal stadium-sized crater
dart-asteroid-crater.body_md:
The crater that NASA's DART spacecraft gouged into the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022 is as big as a stadium, and it is wide enough to have flattened most of the face it hit. That is the first clear view of the scar, taken by Europe's Hera spacecraft, and it was released on Wednesday. It also sits awkwardly against the forecasts made before Hera arrived.

## What Hera saw

DART struck Dimorphos, a small moonlet orbiting the larger asteroid Didymos, on 26 September 2022. The collision shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 32 minutes. It was the first time humans had measurably changed the motion of a natural body in space. DART's own camera died on impact, so nobody has seen the aftermath from close range until now.

Hera, launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) on 7 October 2024, reached the Didymos system in November. Its first pictures, released around 11 November, showed the side of Didymos that DART never imaged. Dimorphos was barely visible, sitting mostly in its parent's shadow. Patrick Michel, Hera's principal investigator, said of that first view: "The first thing we said was wow!"

The later close-ups are more informative. Coverage of the release describes a crater roughly the size of a stadium, spanning much of the asteroid's width. Sabina Raducan, a member of the Hera team, called it "a big crater that is almost as large as the body itself." Away from the crater, ESA says the boulder fields look much as they did in DART's final frames, with no evidence of major changes elsewhere on Dimorphos. Long-exposure images also show hundreds of boulders drifting around the system.

Michael Kueppers, an ESA scientist on the mission, said the impact left Dimorphos "tumbling wildly in its orbit." Some of the boulders near Didymos may be debris thrown across the roughly 1 km gap between the two bodies.

## Why the crater matters

Before Hera arrived, ESA had reported a simulation study suggesting no tidy crater would be found. Dimorphos is thought to be a loosely bound pile of rubble, and the model implied the impact might have reshaped the whole body. The new images fit part of that picture: the crater is huge relative to the asteroid, and the body is clearly disturbed. They do not fit the idea of a wholesale remodelling with no identifiable crater. How the two reconcile is one of the early questions for the team. Only reported coverage was available for this piece; the full ESA release and the underlying images were not checked directly.

The size of the crater matters because of how kinetic impactors work. Hitting an asteroid does not only transfer the spacecraft's momentum. Rock blasted out of the crater leaves in the opposite direction and acts like a thruster, so the total push can exceed what the spacecraft alone delivered. Planners call the multiplier "beta". Estimating it requires knowing how much material left the crater, which depends on the crater's volume and the asteroid's internal strength and mass. Hera can measure both. DART could not.

## What comes next

Hera's close-approach phase is the part that will yield numbers. ESA says the spacecraft is due to come within about 13 km of the asteroid in December, taking higher-resolution images and measuring Dimorphos's mass. Over the following months it will run a dedicated crash-site investigation with its full instrument set.

Those measurements, a mass and a crater volume, are what will let scientists check the roughly 32-minute orbital change against a physical account of where the momentum came from. The answer determines how confidently the same technique could be scaled to a real threat on a different kind of asteroid.

isak-liverpool-brugge.headline: Isak scores twice as Liverpool beat Club Brugge
isak-liverpool-brugge.body_md:
Alexander Isak scored twice as Liverpool won 3-0 at Club Brugge on Wednesday night. It was a comfortable Champions League result, and it gave the striker a night that his season has not often supplied.

The match was played on 25 November. Isak put Liverpool ahead in the 13th minute, punishing a loose pass from the Brugge goalkeeper, Sommer, according to Sky Sports and 101 Great Goals. After that the home side created little. One Lemarechal header, which went too close to Alisson, was the pick of their chances.

## A late flurry

The game was decided in a short spell near the end. Florian Wirtz made it 2-0 in the 79th minute, and Isak added his second three minutes later, in the 82nd. For the first hour or so Liverpool were ahead by a single goal and Brugge were in the game. Two goals in four minutes ended that.

The second goal was also a good one for Wirtz, who has had his own difficulties settling in at Anfield. Liverpool's match report credited both players, headlining the win as one in which Isak and Wirtz "strike".

## What it says about Isak

The case for a striker rediscovering his form rests on thin evidence, and it should be stated as such. Isak's record at Liverpool has been uneven. A December 2025 piece in the search record put his Champions League return at two goals in 14 appearances for the club at that point. That figure predates this season's matches and is not a current tally. A brace, one of the goals from a goalkeeper's error and the other with the game already largely settled, is encouraging rather than conclusive.

It is still the kind of night a forward needs. Isak has had two goals in a game before, in a Premier League win at Ipswich, but a European away fixture is a different test, even against a Brugge side that offered little resistance.

## What's next

Liverpool's next test is the rest of the Champions League league phase, where the points from this win help their position in the table. Reports differ on exactly where it leaves them. Isak's next opportunity to show that this was more than one good evening comes in Liverpool's next league fixture.

andy-taylor-dies.headline: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
andy-taylor-dies.body_md:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist whose riffs gave Duran Duran's early-1980s hits their muscle, has died at 65 after a long battle with prostate cancer. The band said he died on Monday 23 November. Press reports say he died peacefully at home, surrounded by family.

Taylor's cancer became public in November 2022, when Simon Le Bon read out a letter from him at the band's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction. Taylor had been diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. He wrote that it was not immediately life-threatening but that "there is no cure."

## The sound under the sheen

Duran Duran were sold in their heyday on cheekbones, yachts and synthesisers. Taylor was the corrective: a hard-rock-leaning player who gave the polish some bite. On *Rio*, the 1982 album that carried 'Hungry Like the Wolf' and the title track, his guitar kept the songs moving. It is much of the reason they still sound like rock records with a dance-floor habit, and not just the products of a fashion moment.

He belonged to the band's most commercially successful lineup. That was Taylor, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Simon Le Bon, until he left in 1986.

The band's tribute was brief. "Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," the statement said. Le Bon wrote that there was "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it." NME quoted the band as saying his playing "drove the songs that took us around the world."

## Power Station and after

Taylor's most visible detour came in 1985, when he co-formed the supergroup Power Station with Robert Palmer, drummer Tony Thompson and bassist Bernard Edwards. Their cover of 'Some Like It Hot' was a US hit. The project suited his taste for heavier, funk-edged rock, and it also marked the point at which he and Duran Duran began to part ways.

His wife, Tracey, spoke for the family. "To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist," she said, and went on to describe him as a devoted husband, father and grandfather. The family has asked that donations be made in his name to Prostate Cancer UK instead of flowers.

## What survives

The more lasting question is what happens to the catalogue's story. The classic five-piece era is now permanently closed. Reports say Taylor rejoined the band in 2023 to work on the album *Danse Macabre*, which came out that November. That chapter, brief as it was, now reads as a farewell.

The Hall of Fame speech in 2022 remains the clearest picture of how he faced his illness: plain, unsentimental and unsparing about the prognosis. Further tributes from fellow musicians are likely in the days ahead. The family has not yet said whether there will be a public memorial.

richest-man-delays-retirement.headline: Europe's richest man delays retirement until he is 95
richest-man-delays-retirement.body_md:
Bernard Arnault, the 77-year-old chairman and chief executive of LVMH and Europe's richest man, is in no hurry to leave. The Telegraph reports that he intends to delay retirement until he is 95. The figure is eye-catching. The more useful question is how a listed company comes to let one man's birthday be a matter of bylaws.

*A caution on sourcing: The Telegraph article itself could not be read for this piece. What follows rests on the public record of LVMH's age rules, and the 95 figure is attributed to the Telegraph rather than independently confirmed.*

## The mechanism: a rule that keeps moving

The lever is a clause in LVMH's articles of association capping the age of the chairman and chief executive. That cap has been raised twice in quick succession. It stood at 75 until 2022, when shareholders lifted it to 80. In April 2025 the annual meeting raised it again, to 85, with 99.18% of votes cast in favour.

A vote that lopsided says less about persuasion than about structure. The Arnault family controls the group through a holding company, giving it a commanding share of voting rights, so a proposal the family backs is in practice a proposal that passes. Retirement at LVMH is therefore set by the controlling shareholder, ratified by the others.

On the public record, the limit is 85. Reaching 95 would need another change to the bylaws, and another vote, before Arnault turns 85 in 2034. That is an inference from how the rule works, not a detail from the Telegraph.

## What outside investors want

The repeated extensions have not gone unremarked. Arnault has said retirement is not an immediate priority, and investors have pressed for clarity on succession. Some read the move to 85 as a way of postponing a decision, not making one. In January, shareholders were reported to be asking for more transparency about the succession plan.

The family has no shortage of candidates. Arnault's five children hold senior roles across the group. Naming one as heir, or setting out how the choice will be made, is a different matter from tolerating an ever-higher age cap.

The argument for patience is not frivolous. Warren Buffett, then 93, was reported to have written to Arnault warning that an age limit of 80 was a mistake. Founders who built a group of this size tend to be hard to replace. The argument against is that continuity resting on one person's health is a risk, however well he looks.

## What to watch

The next marker is LVMH's annual general meeting in spring, where any further amendment to the age clause would have to appear on the agenda. A resolution to lift the cap past 85 would confirm the Telegraph's account. Its absence would suggest that, for now, the working limit remains 85.

man-utd-sporting-draw.headline: Lammens howler denies Man Utd victory against Sporting in Pochettino's first match
man-utd-sporting-draw.body_md:
Manchester United's search for a first win under Mauricio Pochettino goes on. A 2-2 draw at Sporting in the Champions League on Tuesday night was thrown away in the 80th minute, when goalkeeper Senne Lammens spilled a cross and Luis Suarez hooked in the equaliser.

The result is usually described as Pochettino's first match in charge. That isn't quite right. It was his second. His first, at Liverpool on Sunday, ended in a 4-0 defeat. Pochettino has now taken charge of two games and has conceded two penalties and had two players sent off. The draw is a better result than Anfield, but it still does not feel like progress.

## A match of two goalkeepers' moments

Sporting were awarded a penalty early on, and Lammens saved Suarez's effort in the 31st minute. Seventy-five seconds later he came off his line and clattered Maxi Araujo, and the second penalty was given. Suarez scored it in the 33rd minute.

United were denied an equaliser shortly before half-time. Amad Diallo put the ball in the net, but the referee had already blown for a foul by Youri Tielemans. Sky Sports said Tielemans had won the ball cleanly with a slide tackle, and the whistle meant VAR could not step in. Pochettino called the decision difficult to understand.

Bruno Fernandes levelled it after the break. He converted a penalty in the 48th minute, won when Eduardo Quaresma brought down Lisandro Martinez, then scored again two minutes later. The second was a low shot from distance that bounced off an uneven patch of turf and into the net. It was a soft goal, and United took it.

## The howler, and the goal that wasn't

United held the lead until the 80th minute. A cross dropped into the box, Lammens failed to claim it, and the ball fell to Suarez. He struck it into the net with an acrobatic finish.

United thought they had a late reply. Patrick Dorgu's contact with the goalkeeper, Kaique, led to a corner that Kaique punched into his own net in the 84th minute. After a VAR check, the goal was disallowed. Jamie Carragher called the decision "very harsh." Tielemans was then sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card.

Pochettino was upbeat afterwards. "I'm so proud of the players. It was a tough game," he said. Fernandes was more candid about the goalkeeper. "Mistakes are part of football and from that you get goals," he said, adding that the squad "need to really stick together and understanding that we need to fight for our lives."

## What it means

The sporting cost of one dropped point in the league phase is modest. The managerial cost is harder to measure. Pochettino is two matches into a job he took after United activated his buyout clause earlier this month, and he has inherited a club 19th in the Premier League. Lammens, whose earlier error against Tottenham in October also cost points, is becoming a recurring subject. Two spilled balls and a foul are not a trend on their own, but United do not have much margin.

The next test is at home to Brentford on Saturday. It offers Pochettino a chance to get his first win at Old Trafford, and Lammens a chance to put a bad night behind him.

milburn-youth-unemployment-cost.headline: Treasury raises cost concerns over Milburn youth unemployment plan
milburn-youth-unemployment-cost.body_md:
The Treasury has pushed back on the cost of parts of Alan Milburn's review of youth unemployment. That turns a report about young people out of work into a test of how much room the government actually has to spend. The Guardian's report, which this article draws on, gives no figures for the Treasury's objection. Nor does it include a Treasury quote or say how large its concerns are.

## What Milburn proposed

Milburn, a former health secretary, published his review in mid-November. It focuses on the roughly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training, the group known as NEETs. He argues the system needs a "complete system reset", according to [The Week's summary](https://theweek.com/business/jobs/the-milburn-report-five-key-takeaways).

The main recommendations are:

- **A legal guarantee.** Young people unemployed for more than 12 months would be entitled to a six-month placement, training or employment support, delivered through a Youth Opportunity Service in England. Those who refuse could lose benefits.
- **Benefit changes.** Under-25s would lose the health element of universal credit and personal independence payments. A new "youth allowance" at the standard universal credit rate would replace them. Milburn accepts that some young people could be worse off at first.
- **A hiring subsidy.** Employers would receive a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant for taking on someone who has been out of work for six months or more. The estimated cost is £5.8bn a year. Milburn offsets that with £3.6bn in welfare savings and £2.4bn in extra tax revenue and lower benefit payments. Critics say the net saving is nearer £200m a year.
- **Employer National Insurance.** The review recommends reversing the employer contribution increases for workers aged 21 to 24. Retail and hospitality provide almost 40% of under-25 jobs.

## Where the Treasury objects

The clearest reported resistance is on National Insurance. [Retail Week](https://www.retail-week.com/people/treasury-resists-milburns-key-national-insurance-costs-reduction-proposal/7052672.article) reported on 19 November that the Treasury opposes this recommendation, which retailers widely welcomed. The article is paywalled, so the Treasury's reasoning is not visible. [UnHerd](https://unherd.com/newsroom/milburn-review-wont-rescue-britain-from-its-welfare-trap/?set_edition=en) describes the review as proposing to double the employer threshold for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000, but only when the Treasury judges the public finances allow it. That condition is already a concession to the Treasury's veto.

The wider spending ask is larger. Other coverage, including [City AM](https://www.cityam.com/?p=2478826), says the review tells the Chancellor to find billions more. Milburn has called for a "radical reprioritisation" of Whitehall spending. The Irish News put the package at [£58bn a year](https://www.irishnews.com/news/uk/burnham-challenged-to-back-58bn-a-year-reforms-to-tackle-youth-unemployment-WGZXEQ5VMVOKXBON3BCSZVDGSA/), and the review attributes a £125bn annual cost to the current system. I could not confirm how those figures relate to one another. They should be read as claims, not as a settled Treasury costing.

## Why the dispute matters

Milburn's case is that spending now pays back later. Reports say he projects higher employment adding to growth and tax receipts, and that welfare savings would not begin until 2029. A 10-year programme with costs up front and savings later is hard for a Treasury that is protecting thin headroom against its fiscal rules.

That is why the argument matters beyond one report. Which departmental proposals survive contact with the Treasury is a guide to how tight the headroom really is. It also decides whether young people out of work see the guarantee, the grant and the National Insurance cut, or only some of them.

## What to watch

The test is how much of the package the government adopts and when. Ministers have been reported to be weighing a slower rise in the youth minimum wage. The next signal is a formal government response to the review, and whether it sets out costings, particularly for the National Insurance change.
